title: Polynomial-time private convex-hull point selection
formal: Do there exist a randomized algorithm \(A\) and fixed polynomials \(p,q\) with the following guarantees? For all integers \(d\ge1\), \(X\ge2\), privacy and failure parameters \(0<\varepsilon\le1\), \(0<\delta,\beta<1/3\), and finite datasets \(S=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\) from \[G_{d,X}=\{0,1/X,2/X,\ldots,1\}^{d},\] if \[n\ge p\!\left(d,\lceil\log_2(X+1)\rceil,1/\varepsilon,\log(1/\delta),\log(1/\beta)\right),\] the algorithm returns a point in \(\operatorname{conv}(S)\) with probability at least \(1-\beta\), is \((\varepsilon,\delta)\)-differentially private for replacement of one input point, and uses at most \[q\!\left(n,d,\lceil\log_2(X+1)\rceil,1/\varepsilon,\log(1/\delta),\log(1/\beta)\right)\] operations in the arithmetic and sampling model below. All constants and polynomial degrees are independent of the parameters and the input. The output may lie outside the grid. This is the source's question about polynomial computation with a sample threshold polynomial in dimension and grid bit length, with the privacy and success parameters exposed.
why: Private selection of a convex combination is a basic geometric feasibility primitive. Without privacy the task is trivial, but a private algorithm must avoid revealing any one input point while still returning an exactly feasible point on degenerate data. Its connection to private linear inequalities and halfspace learning makes polynomial dependence on dimension consequential.
status_note: Resolved positively in the arithmetic/sampling model by Kaplan–Mansour–Moran–Stemmer–Tur, published at STOC 2025; full-version Corollary 25 and the numerical-model caveat were checked on 15 September 2026. The finite-bit implementation is suggested rather than established in that manuscript and is not claimed here.

progress.text: Theorem 5.1 obtains an \(O(n^{d})\)-time private algorithm and §6 asks for polynomial dependence with dimension-independent exponent and polynomial sample threshold.

The full author manuscript of On Differentially Private Linear Algebra supplies the positive arithmetic-model result; Corollary 25 states the exact grid-selection and success guarantee. The numeric-model caveat is stated on p. 5.
The result is published in STOC 2025, pp. 2362–2373.

Matched the published result and its full-version theorem against the original grid, sample threshold, degeneracy, privacy, output and runtime requirements. The original arithmetic-model question is resolved and is archived; no claim is made to have formalized its proof or verified the suggested finite-precision implementation.

importance.reason: A foundational geometric feasibility primitive connected to private linear programming and halfspace learning. The historical high-dimensional computation barrier was substantial; its now-published resolution belongs in the archive rather than the open benchmark.

sentences: The input is a private collection of points on a public finite grid.
The task asks for one point in their convex hull, including when the hull is lower-dimensional.
The historical question required both computation and the sufficient sample threshold to remain polynomial in dimension and grid bit length.
A published STOC 2025 result resolves this in the exact-arithmetic and continuous-sampling model, with polynomial dependence on dimension.
The archived review preserves that positive result and explicitly separates it from the manuscript’s unproved suggestion of a finite-precision implementation.

definitions: A dataset is a finite list and can contain repetitions. Adjacent datasets have the same length and agree at every position except possibly one; \(d,X,n,\varepsilon,\delta,\beta\) are public. The convex hull is \(\operatorname{conv}(S)=\{\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lambda_i x_i:\lambda_i\ge0,\ \sum_i\lambda_i=1\}\); lower-dimensional and degenerate inputs are included. The output space is \(\mathbb R^{d}\cup\{\bot\}\), where \(\bot\) denotes failure. For every adjacent pair of datasets of a qualifying length and every Borel event \(E\) in that space, privacy means \(\Pr[A(S)\in E]\le e^{\varepsilon}\Pr[A(S')\in E]+\delta\). The probability includes all internal sampling. No convex-hull vertex list, general-position promise, interior-volume promise, or lower bound on distances is supplied. The computation model is a uniform finite program with exact real registers and ordinary integer control, unit-cost arithmetic \(+,-,\times,\div\) (nonzero divisors), comparisons, nonnegative square roots, logarithms and exponentials on their domains, and independent standard uniform and Laplace real draws; a Laplace draw has density \(e^{-|z|}/2\). Explicit loops, storage operations, and arithmetic operations all count. The bound is worst-case in the number of these operations; failure probability covers randomized unsuccessful execution. This is an ideal arithmetic/sampling convention matching the geometric sources, not a proved finite-bit implementation. Dependence on \(\log X\) is allowed, so the statement is not a strongly polynomial bound independent of coordinate precision. The source's fixed-privacy formulation is represented with polynomial dependence on reciprocal \(\varepsilon\) and logarithmic dependence on the two failure parameters, as in its later resolution.
answer_criterion: Give a uniform algorithm and polynomials \(p,q\), together with a Lean-checked proof of its full privacy inequality, success probability, and operation bound on every qualifying grid dataset; or prove that no such algorithm and polynomials exist in the stated model. Producing an arbitrary input record, an approximately feasible point, or a guarantee only for full-dimensional datasets does not meet the criterion. A positive result in this arithmetic/sampling model does not by itself prove a bit-complexity theorem.

source_formulation.text: Is polynomial-time private convex-hull point selection possible when the sample size remains polynomial in the dimension and in the logarithm of the grid resolution?
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase

context_blocks.text: The input coordinates come from a public finite grid. The problem is to produce just one point in the convex hull, rather than disclose a hull description or all extreme points. Releasing one of the records always solves the nonprivate geometric task, but in general violates the stability requirement imposed by privacy.

The sample-size requirement is essential. The original paper distinguishes the actual number of input points from the minimum dataset size required for a uniform success guarantee. Its open-question parenthesis requires that this threshold stay polynomial in dimension and in the logarithm of the grid resolution; an algorithm requiring exponentially many records would not answer that question.

The 2020 algorithm takes \(O(n^{d})\) time in its geometric model, with sample threshold \(\Omega(d^{4}\log(dX/\delta)/\varepsilon)\) and success at least \(1-\delta\). This is polynomial for fixed dimension but has a dimension-dependent exponent. It handles degeneracy, which matters because deep regions can have zero ambient volume.

Kaplan, Mansour, Moran, Stemmer and Tur give a polynomial-time arithmetic algorithm for the same point-selection task. Their full-version Corollary 25 has sample threshold \(d^{17}/\varepsilon\) times a polynomial in logarithms of \(d,1/\beta,1/\delta,X\). Its grid \(\{-1,-1+1/X,\ldots,1\}^{d}\) contains the original nonnegative grid. Add/remove privacy in that framework implies replacement privacy after constant-factor parameter rescaling. This resolves the original polynomial-existence barrier, without claiming an optimal sample exponent.

The resolution explicitly assumes arbitrary-precision numerical operations, continuous noise and square roots. Its authors state that they believe finite-precision implementation is possible by standard discretizations; the checked manuscript does not supply that implementation. The archived claim is therefore limited to the arithmetic/sampling model stated here. This restriction is separate from the published positive mathematical and algorithmic resolution.
